title: Accompanying the dying
hook: being present, saying the Shema, holding a hand
tomorrow: after a loss, why does Jewish mourning hand you a schedule?

segments.voice: That was a week of growing older: a task for every age, standing for the hoary head, the surgeon and the prayer, the carer, a letter of values, a plan said out loud. Yesterday's line: a kindness to them.
screen: `A KINDNESS TO THEM.` → `A WEEK OF GROWING OLDER.`

segments.voice: A hospice hallway. Soft shoes, a cart going by, a door left half open. Somewhere inside, someone you love is near the end, and the question pounding in your chest is: what do I say? Here's the gentle news from the tradition. The words matter less than you think. What matters is that you go in.
screen: `A DOOR LEFT HALF OPEN.` → `WHAT DO I SAY?` → `GO IN.`

segments.voice: When Jacob goes down to Egypt, God promises him in a dream that his son will be with him at the end: "and Joseph shall put his hand upon thine eyes." The promise isn't a speech. It's a hand. Years later, Jacob dies surrounded by his sons, after speaking to each. Jewish custom carries that closeness forward. Tradition asks that a dying person not be left alone. Those with them may help them say a short confession, or say for them the line the prayer book sets for morning and night: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." And when no words come at all, a hand held is enough. Every line from this week meets in that room. The later years have their task, even now. You rise for the one in the bed. Doctors and prayer, together. The carers there are holy. Values already passed on. Wishes already known, so nobody is guessing. All that's left is to be present.
screen: `JOSEPH'S HAND UPON HIS EYES.` · `NOT LEFT ALONE.` · `HEAR, O ISRAEL.` · `THE WEEK MEETS IN THAT ROOM.` · then, large: `BE PRESENT.`

segments.voice: If someone is with you, hold their hand, and say nothing. If you're alone, rest one hand inside the other and feel its warmth. Keep a person in mind, near or far, who needs someone beside them, and stay with them in your thoughts.
Accompanying the dying: staying close, saying the Shema or nothing at all, and holding a hand, so no one goes alone.
Your line: be present; a hand held says what words can't. Take good care of yourself tonight.
